original_quote: The dissemination of antimicrobial resistance can be described as a two-step process. First, de-novo mutations or acquisition of resistance genes, or both, occurs via mobile genetic elements, such as plasmids mediating an antimicrobial-resistance phenotype. Second, antimicrobial resistance contagion—the spread of resistant strains—proceeds via several vectors (eg, human beings, insects, birds, agriculture, and water). Selection pressure caused by antibiotic consumption is an important primary factor not only for the de-novo emergence of antimicrobial resistance but also for the selective multiplication of resistant bacteria. Reducing inappropriate antibiotic consumption is a recognised policy priority, and substantial efforts are focused on controlling antibiotic usage volumes in hospitals, the community, and the agricultural sector. Although antibiotic usage has been shown to be an important driver for increasing antimicrobial resistance levels, the spread of resistant bacteria or the genes that encode for resistance are likely to be much more important in the dissemination and prevalence of antimicrobial resistance. The environment (including transmission via water, insects, animals, and birds) plays an underappreciated part in the development and spread of resistant bacteria. title: Seasonal variations in antibiotic resistance genes in estuarine sediments and the driving mechanisms
original_quote: Under the effects of chemical pollutants (organic pollutants and heavy metals), the number and abundance of estuarine sediment ARGs significantly increased (Fig.2)... Compared with SDS and WDS, the number of different estuarine sediment ARGs increased by 76.9%–92.3% in summer and 5.9%–35.3% in winter, and the abundance of these ARGs increased by 29–5195 times in summer and 48–239 times in winter. (Results-p.5); "The abundance levels of sediment ARGs in the Oujiang and Feiyunjiang estuaries were higher in winter than in summer, while the abundance of sediment ARGs in the Aojiang estuary was approximately three orders of magnitude lower in winter than in summer (Fig.2)." (Results-p.5); "In the Oujiang estuary sediments, the concentrations of organic pollutants, heavy metals and antibiotics reached a maximum of 0.536 μg g−1, 629.09 mg kg-1 and 355.2 μg kg-1 in summer and 0.483 μg g−1, 580.27 mg kg-1 and 325.69 μg kg-1 in winter, respectively. Furthermore, the pollutant concentrations of estuarine sediments were higher in summer than in winter. Comparing summer with winter, the concentrations of organic pollutants, heavy metals and antibiotics increased by 0.053 μg g−1, 48.82 mg kg-1 and 29.51 μg kg-1 in the Oujiang estuary sediments, by 0.042 μg g−1, 36.93 mg kg-1 and 14.43 μg kg-1 in the Aojiang sediments, and by 0.044 μg g−1, 37.89 mg kg-1 and 16.13 μg kg-1 in the Feiyunjiang estuary sediments." (Results-p.5); "The difference in abiotic factors during summer and winter may be part of the reason for more pollutants in estuarine sediments during summer. The environmental conditions such as seasonal differences in sunlight and seawater temperature, as well as floods and red tides that are prone to bursting in summer, may cause an increase of pollutants in the estuary sediments, which subsequently influences the abundance of estuarine sediment ARGs. First of all, the sunlight intensity in the Wenzhou region is stronger in summer than in winter and the illumination time is also longer than in winter, which makes seawater temperatures higher in summer than in winter. This makes summer more favorable for the chemical reaction of pollutants in seawater and a large number of secondary pollutants are produced. Subsequently, this causes more contaminants to settle into sediments, thereby increasing contaminants in sediments. Furthermore, the precipitation in the Wenzhou region is greater in summer than in winter, which makes it easy to cause an outbreak of flooding in summer. The flood carries a large amount of pollutants into the river and then enters the estuary, thus increasing the pollutants in the estuary sediments. Last but not least, the coastal waters in the Wenzhou region are prone to red tides in summer, and a large number of toxic pollutants are released during the red tide outbreak. In the central part of the lake, we also found plasmid-bearing bacteria with no more than two plasmids. title: Geographical and seasonal distribution of multiple antibiotic resistance of heterotrophic bacteria of Lake Shira

original_quote: From the data presented in Figure 4 it is also obvious that in the central part of the lake the heterotrophic bacteria are represented by halotolerant (25–30%) and halophile (47–66%) forms, while in the resort area freshwater (20–40%) and halophile (55–75%) bacteria were dominant. In the cells of Micrococcus sp. This allows suggesting that the plasmid of 2.7 kb is of primary importance for survival of freshwater microorganisms in the brackish Shira lake." (Results-p.4); "A much more dense cell wall accompanied the increase of resistance of halotolerant bacteria. title: Geographical and seasonal distribution of multiple antibiotic resistance of heterotrophic bacteria of Lake Shira

title: Multiple antibiotic resistance of heterotrophic bacteria in the littoral zone of Lake Shira as an indicator of human impact on the ecosystem
pathogen: 湖泊近岸带异养细菌(Aeromonas, Citrobacter, Vibrio, E. coli, Enterococcus, Sarcina等)
original_quote: It has been found that in Summer, human and animal microflora featuring multiple antibiotic resistance (to Ampicillin and Kanamycin) predominates in all the studied stations of the littoral zone of the lake. In Spring, concentrations of bacteria featuring multiple antibiotic resistance decrease significantly and bacteria sensitive to antibiotics predominate in the lake. Emergence of multiple antibiotic resistance in bacteria of Lake Shira is caused by the input of allochthonous bacteria into the lake; this feature of heterotrophic bacteria of Lake Shira can be used to monitor the impact on the ecosystem made by health resorts. (Abstract); "We examined bacteria isolated from samples collected at different stations of the littoral zone in Summer and did not find any bacteria sensitive to antibiotics even at stations situated far from the close-to-resort part. Concentrations of bacteria featuring multiple antibiotic resistance registered at Stations 3–7, which are infrequently visited by vacationers, and at Stations 8–12, which are inaccessible to vacationers, were comparable to concentrations of such bacteria at Stations 1, 2, 13 and 14, which are situated near the tourist camps, and at Station 16, situated near the resorts. In the central part of Lake Shira (Station 21), the levels of bacteria displaying multiple antibiotic resistance were similar to those registered in the close-to-resort zone (Station 16). High concentrations of bacteria resistant to Ampicillin and Kanamycin in the parts of the littoral zone that are either not frequented by vacationers or are inaccessible to them and in the central part of Lake Shira can probably be a result of transport of such bacteria with the water from the parts of the lake that suffer most from human impact." (Discussion-p.4); "In Spring, when anthropogenic input is very small, bacteria sensitive to antibiotics and bacteria only resistant to Ampicillin predominated in the littoral zone of the lake. Bacteria displaying multiple antibiotic resistance were mainly isolated from the part of the lake receiving resort waste effluents (Station 19), the resort part (Station 18) and the area where tourist camps are situated (Station 13). The bacteria resistant to Ampicillin and Kanamycin that were isolated from samples collected at Station 19 were of Enterococcus and Sarcina spp. and at Stations 13 and 18 – of Enterococcus sp. The water samples collected from the littoral part of Lake Shira that is inaccessible to tourists (Stations 3 and 5) and from the central part of the lake contained bacteria featuring multiple antibiotic resistance." (Results-p.3); "The main reason why Enterococcus and Sarcina spp. occur in the lake in Spring, when human impact on the ecosystem is very low, may be that these bacteria, contained in vertebrates' feces, enter the lake with snowmelt runoff." (Discussion-p.6)

original_quote: Contamination of the littoral part of the lake with allochthonous bacteria is potentially dangerous to the ecosystem because this is the zone where bacteria can survive by attaching themselves to sediment particles. An et al. (2001), conducted their studies at Lake Texoma and found that concentrations of E. coli and total coliforms increased with depth and their maximal concentrations were registered in water samples collected from the bottom layer of water, because bacteria were associated with lake-bottom sediments. Comparison of reduction rates of microbial indicators (E. coli, enterococci, fecal coliforms) in the water and sediment of a brackish water body (Lake Pontchartrain) also showed that the reduction rate of indicator organisms in sediment was slower. The authors assumed that the reason was attachment of microbial indicators to sediment. Thus, bottom sediment may act as a reservoir for prolonging indicator organism survival, which adds concern of recontamination of overlaying waters due to potential solids resuspension. pathogen: 水体微生物(携带ARGs的细菌)
original_quote: Metals and antibiotics accelerate the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB)-carrying antibiotic-resistance genes (ARGs) by exerting selective pressure on bacteria, which in turn exacerbates the spread of ARGs in the ecosystem. Cr, Cu, Cd, Pb, and Zn released from industrial emissions, agricultural activities, and transportation pollution enter the environment through rainwater runoff, atmospheric deposition, and other pathways. These heavy metals showed different correlations with ARGs. Cd was positively correlated with tetX and tetA, but negatively correlated with sul2 (Figures 4 and 5). Cd induces oxidative stress in bacterial cells, activating efflux pumps like tetA and tetX, which expel tetracyclines, promoting bacterial survival and increasing ARG prevalence. In contrast, Cd inhibits sulfur metabolism in sulfate-reducing bacteria, potentially reducing sul2 gene abundance. Additionally, Cd interferes with biofilm formation, further hindering the proliferation of sulfonamide-resistant bacteria. Cr was significantly positively correlated with sul1 and tetE; Cu and Zn were positively correlated with tetX and tetD; and Pb was positively correlated with sul1, tetA, and tetC, but possibly negatively correlated with tetE (Figures 4 and 5). Cr, particularly Cr(VI), induces oxidative stress, triggering DNA damage and promoting the transfer of resistance genes like sul1 and tetE via integrase activity, enhancing gene spread in bacterial communities exposed to chronic Cr stress. Cu and Zn generate reactive oxygen species, prompting bacteria to upregulate efflux pumps like tetX and tetD to expel metals and antibiotics, facilitating bacterial survival under metal stress. Metal tolerance genes and antibiotic resistance genes often reside on the same plasmids or integrons, promoting co-selection and increasing the likelihood of resistance in contaminated environments. Pb causes oxidative damage and can select bacteria that tolerate stress, co-selecting sul1, tetA, and tetC resistance genes due to their association with mobile genetic elements. The negative correlation between Pb and tetE may arise from specific microbial community dynamics or interference with conjugation mechanisms, shifting the resistance profile toward other mechanisms. Thus, Pb could select alternative resistance strategies, reducing the prominence of tetE. These heavy metals alter the microbial community structure, and heavy metals with substantial toxicity and antioxidant properties, such as Cr, trigger microbial stress responses, selectively promote the proliferation of drug-resistant bacteria, enhance the adaptability of bacteria-harboring resistance genes, and promote the spread of resistance genes. (Discussion-p.14-15)
